title: Burn-Lot Exit Desk for Fire Survivors
one_liner: Package burned lots and stranded insurance claims into sellable assets, and auction them to vetted builders at fair prices.
customer: Owners of destroyed lots in the Palisades and Altadena (free to them). Builders, small developers and community land trusts pay a success fee.
problem: About 13% of affected Palisades single-family owners have started rebuilding 18-plus months on. Insurer estimates ($462/sq ft) sit far below contractor budgets (up to $1,065). Many owners do not want to become developers, and cash buyers lowball lots.
solution: Prepare each lot as a marketable asset: claim documents (what transfers and what does not), debris and utility status, pre-approved plans and permit history. Run a competitive bid among vetted builders with three options: sell the lot, sell with claim assignment, or take a fixed-price turnkey rebuild. Handle escrow and title through partners.
why_now: Deadlines on additional-living-expense coverage and permit pipelines are biting 18 months after the fires, and the low rebuild rate shows demand for an exit.
revenue_model: A 2-3% buyer-paid success fee, builder subscriptions for deal flow, and later turnkey rebuild margin.
non_obvious_insight: 'Rebuilding services' is the obvious market. The larger one is liquidity: turning a lot plus a claim into cash at a fair price.
first_30_days: Interview 30 owners in fire-survivor groups, recruit 3 builders, and hand-run 5 lots. Use a licensed broker partner for the transaction side.

title: Memory Budget CI for Game Studios
one_liner: CI tooling and fixed-fee audits that enforce RAM and VRAM budgets per target device, because the assumption that hardware gets better each generation just broke.
customer: Mid-size PC and console studios (30-300 staff) shipping in 2027 to Steam Deck, Switch 2 and 8-16GB PCs.
problem: AI data centers are absorbing the RAM supply. Valve's Steam Machine launched at $1,049 against an early target of about $800, Xbox prices rose, and Switch 2 goes to $499.99 on 2026-09-01. The installed base will stay at today's memory ceilings for years, but studios budget memory as a fixed cap and find regressions in late QA.
solution: An Unreal, Unity and Godot CI plugin that builds against device memory profiles, snapshots per-level memory, attributes growth to specific assets and pull requests, and suggests fixes (texture format changes, streaming pool sizes, audio bank downsampling). Sold alongside a 3-week 'memory diet' audit that finds duplicated and unstripped assets.
why_now: Memory vendors now quote a monthly price and a yes-or-no on volume, per a Valve engineer. Console and handheld price hikes in 2026 mean players will not upgrade into new game requirements. Studios are planning holiday 2026-27 lineups now.
revenue_model: $15-40k per audit, $400-2,500 per month per studio for CI, and later a subscription to a device-profile and min-spec benchmark database.
non_obvious_insight: The industry's optimization culture is about frame time. When hardware gets pricier over its life, the cheapest way to grow the addressable market is to shrink footprint, and most footprint is asset-pipeline waste that can be found and fixed automatically.
first_30_days: Publish an analysis of Steam minimum-spec trends versus the Hardware Survey to get inbound. Ship a free open-source memory snapshot diff tool for Unity and Unreal. Offer free audits to 5 studios in exchange for case studies, and convert 2 into paid engagements.

title: Second-Look Verification for Imagery-Based Nonrenewals
one_liner: A $50-80, 48-hour human check between an aerial-imagery flag and a nonrenewal, sold to carriers' compliance teams.
customer: Regional and mid-size homeowners carriers and MGAs in California, Connecticut, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania and New York, bought by underwriting and compliance leads.
problem: Imagery-driven nonrenewals are generating regulatory heat (a Florida owner with 52 claim-free years was dropped with no inspection). California AB 75 became operative July 1 2026, requiring notice, a copy of the photos, a dispute path and a remediation window. CT, NH and PA regulators say imagery alone is insufficient, and a NY bill is pending. In-person inspections cost far more and take weeks.
solution: A guided homeowner video capture with fraud checks, or a local gig inspector, returning structured findings mapped to the carrier's rules. It auto-generates the compliant notice package and remediation checklist, and keeps an audit log for regulators.
why_now: AB 75 took effect July 1 2026, and other states are moving.
revenue_model: Per flagged policy plus a platform fee.
non_obvious_insight: Regulators demand more than imagery, but nobody wants $250 inspections. The lower price point makes compliance affordable at scale and sells to a budget-holding compliance team.
first_30_days: Call 10 regional carriers' compliance heads and pilot with 200 flagged policies. Prove the share of imagery flags that human review clears.

title: Flight simulator drills for county SNAP eligibility workers
one_liner: Short daily drills using synthetic cases built from the state's own error taxonomy, sold to county social-services directors who are about to pay for every eligibility mistake.
customer: County social services / DSS directors and supervisors in county-administered SNAP states (NY, NC, CA, OH, MN, CO, VA) and the state associations of counties. Buyers pay $12k-25k per county per year, or $150-300 per worker. States can buy statewide at $150k-500k.
problem: H.R.1 raises the state/county share of SNAP administrative costs from 50% to 75% starting October 2026. From October 2027, states with payment error rates of 6% or higher must pay part of benefit costs. In New York, St. Lawrence County faces an extra $776,000 in year one, Jefferson County over $1 million and Warren County $415,000. The state's error rate is 13% against a 6% line, a penalty of about $1B statewide, described as 'a missile heading right at New York State'. North Carolina's error rate is 6.69%, with state cost-share exposure of about $140M at 5% and $420M at 15%. The state's advice to counties is 'documenting, documenting, documenting'.
solution: A 15-minute daily micro-drill for eligibility workers: a synthetic household case (pay stubs, shelter costs, household composition changes, address changes) with a realistic case-file packet, where the worker computes eligibility and benefit. The drill feeds back the exact error that federal QC would cite. Cases are generated from the state's policy manual and the public USDA QC error categories (wage reporting, household size, address changes and shelter deductions are the common ones), with no real client data. Supervisors see per-worker error-type heatmaps and a coaching queue. Later: an optional second-look review desk staffed by former QC reviewers that samples a county's real closed cases.
why_now: The error-rate look-back, cost-shift start (October 2026) and penalty tiers (October 2027) create a hard two-year clock. Louisiana is paying cash bonuses to error spotters, Kansas hired an outside consultant, Virginia is buying technology for error checking, and NC is running monthly QC webinars and targeting high-error counties. States are visibly buying error-reduction help, and there is no standard product for it.
revenue_model: Per-worker annual subscription ($150-300) or flat per-county fee ($12k-25k); statewide contracts through the state SNAP office or county association; add-on per-case second-look review at $18-30/case.
non_obvious_insight: A county with a 0% error rate is still penalized if the state averages above 6%, so no county can solve this alone and the real buyer is the state or the association pooling county money. Meanwhile individual county directors are hurting now and have discretionary admin budgets and training budgets they can spend without an RFP. Synthetic cases avoid the PII and system-access barrier that blocks most govtech vendors in benefits programs, so a small team can start selling in weeks, not after a FedRAMP-style review. Evidence: county exposure and 13% New York error rate (https://www.northcountrypublicradio.org/news/story/53929/20260910/snap-cost-shift-pushes-north-country-counties-into-a-financial-bind); NC official on documentation, targeted training and CQI (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9949745/north-carolina/executive/organizations/state-departments-and-agencies/mental-health/developmental-disabilities-and-substance-abuse-services/state-official-urges-counties-to-cut-snap-payment-error-rate-to-avoid-hr1-cost-shares); state remediation tactics such as bonuses, outside consultants and new training (https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/states-scramble-cut-snap-error-214614305.html).
first_30_days: Build 40 synthetic cases across the top error elements from one state's manual, with a scoring engine. Approach the state county association's SNAP resource group and 5 county DSS directors with a free 30-day pilot with a pre/post test on 10 new hires. Publish a 'your error rate in dollars' calculator for county commissioners. Convert the two most engaged counties to paid annual plans priced below their discretionary-purchase limits.

title: Battery passport starter that feeds on repair-shop events
one_liner: A cheap battery-passport package for e-bike and small pack makers, plus a repair-shop scanning app that supplies the lifecycle events the passport is legally supposed to track.
customer: Small and mid-size European e-bike, e-scooter and cargo-bike brands, pack assemblers, and industrial or storage battery integrators above 2 kWh. The battery passport must exist from 18 Feb 2027. Independent repair shops and refurbishers are the second user group.
problem: From 18 Feb 2027, LMT, EV and industrial batteries over 2 kWh need a passport reachable by QR code and linked to a unique identifier. The Annex XIII list has 71 entries, but 'not every field is due in February 2027': fields are day-one, modelled-now-populated-later, or waiting on secondary legislation. Access-rights rules are slipping to Q4 2026 and key standards are still in draft. Passports must track state of health, cycle counts and status changes after repurposing or remanufacturing. As one guide says, 'a once-published PDF or marketing microsite is not enough'. Enterprise passport platforms are priced for large firms with compliance teams.
solution: Two products. (1) A brand starter package: a field-status mapper that says which of the 71 fields are due now, later or pending; ISO/IEC 15459-style unique ID and QR generation; a hosted passport page; and a written-authorisation template so the brand can legally delegate passport management to us. (2) A free repair-shop and refurbisher app that scans the QR, logs state-of-health tests, cell swaps, cycle data and second-life events, and pushes them into the brand's passport. Shops get a free workflow tool and repair leads. Brands pay for the passport and the event stream. This also lines up with the replaceable-battery rule that applies from 18 Feb 2027 and with the Right to Repair Directive.
why_now: The passport deadline is under 5 months away and the access-rights implementing act is late. Replaceable portable batteries and e-bike batteries become an obligation on the same date. Eighteen Member States had not notified full transposition of the Right to Repair Directive by September 2026, which leaves national repair rules unsettled while shops still have to service batteries.
revenue_model: Brand setup of EUR 2-5k. Subscription of roughly EUR 1-3 per battery per year (or a EUR 300-1,500 per month floor). Optional per-event fee for verified state-of-health tests. Later, a paid API for insurers and second-life buyers.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone sells 'publish a QR page'. The law's real burden is a lifecycle record kept consistent across systems and updated when the battery is serviced or repurposed, and that happens in repair shops that no passport vendor serves. Evidence: 'The hard part is not publishing a page. The hard part is keeping model-level, plant-level, and individual-battery records consistent', passports must track state of health, cycle counts and status changes, and batteries allow the operator to authorise another actor in writing to manage the passport (https://infodpp.eu/en/blog/battery-dpp-deadline-february-2027/). Mid-scale companies are named as the likely pressure point (https://www.batterytechonline.com/design-manufacturing/preparing-for-eu-battery-qr-code-standards-in-2027) and passport software is described as badly priced for small manufacturers (https://dpp-tool.com/en/guide/dpp-software-comparison/). Replaceability and spare-battery availability from 18 Feb 2027 are covered at https://www.intertek.com/blog/2025/06-27-2027-reqs-for-removability-and-replaceability-of-batteries-in-electrical-products/. Right to Repair transposition gap: https://www.eunews.it/en/2026/09/25/right-to-repair-italy-and-17-other-countries-have-failed-to-transpose-the-directive-eu-infringement-proceedings-begin/.
first_30_days: Build a spreadsheet-based field-status mapper for the 71 fields and offer it as a free download. Contact 30 small e-bike brands and pack assemblers found through European trade fairs, cycling industry associations and importer lists. Sell 3 paid 'passport readiness sprint' engagements at EUR 1.5-3k each that end with a hosted pilot passport for one battery model. In parallel, recruit 10 independent e-bike shops to test the scan-and-log app on real service jobs.

title: Bale Grade Audits With Premium Sharing
one_liner: Independent PET and HDPE bale audits, plus MRF line tuning paid from the price uplift, to turn 'commodity bales' into measured, spec-priced material.
customer: Independent MRFs selling plastic bales (pay a share of uplift) and the surviving US reclaimers, who pay for supplier scoring and dispute referee services.
problem: Feedstock PET bales hit 1.44 cents/lb in April 2026 and seven of about 30 US reclaimers closed. Yet New Jersey delayed its food-contact PCR mandate citing constrained food-grade supply, while recyclers say HDPE blow-mold supply is 'not constrained.' That points to a quality-tier mismatch, not a shortage.
solution: Third-party bale audits (manual composition sort, handheld NIR, moisture and weight) that produce a bale spec sheet. A tuning playbook for optical-sorter recipes and QC pickers. Contracts that pay MRFs on measured tier and give reclaimers a lot-level dispute referee.
why_now: The 2026 price collapse and reclaimer closures leave the remaining buyers desperate for predictable quality. The mandate delays mean brands cannot lock supply, so spec-priced material becomes the negotiating currency.
revenue_model: $150-400 per audited load, plus 25-35% of documented price uplift for 6-12 months, plus an annual supplier-scoring subscription for reclaimers.
non_obvious_insight: The 'shortage' insiders cite is a shortage of known-quality material. A measured bale is a different commodity, and no third party captures the gap between 1.44 cents and reclaimer-grade pricing because no one measures it.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 independent MRFs and 1 reclaimer. Manually audit 30 bales and publish the anonymized quality spread. Offer a 6-month uplift-share deal. Buy or borrow a handheld NIR ($10-25K) and standardize the photo protocol.

title: Bonded Claims: Bug Bounties for Product Labels
one_liner: Brands post a forfeitable bond behind a testable label claim, and anyone can buy the product, get it lab-tested and collect the bond if the claim is false.
customer: Mid-size DTC supplement, protein, baby-food and pet-food brands whose 'third-party tested' or 'heavy-metal free' claims are doubted, plus retail and marketplace buyers who want evidence and insurers.
problem: Label claims cannot be checked on the shelf. Certifications are one-time and paid for by the certified. Heavy-metal and potency class actions are routine, and gray-market peptide vendors forge certificates of analysis (FDA warning letters to seven online sellers, Mar 2026). Honest brands cannot distinguish themselves.
solution: A claim registry. The brand states a specific, machine-checkable claim (for example lead below X per serving, or label potency within 10%), posts a $10-50k bond in escrow and accepts a protocol: retail-purchased units, an accredited lab, and blinded replicates. Challengers pay for tests or use subsidised credits, and a neutral panel confirms chain of custody. A failed claim pays the challenger and forfeits the bond and badge. A claim that survives N challenges earns a 'survived challenge' tier that retail buyers can query by API.
why_now: Finnrick has now published 10,000+ independent peptide tests, proving that crowds will fund lab tests of vendors. Heavy-metal exposés and lawsuits keep recurring. Stablecoin and card-hold escrow make small bonds cheap to run. Retailers want a liability shield for clean-label shelves.
revenue_model: $2-5k annual listing fee, a 1-3% bond-management fee, challenge-processing fees, and retailer API licences.
non_obvious_insight: Bug bounties worked in software because they turn hostile sceptics into paid auditors. Physical-goods certification does the opposite and pays friendly auditors. A bond makes the brand fund the scepticism, and only honest brands can afford to post one, which gives the badge a real price premium.
first_30_days: Approach 10 clean-label brands that already publish certificates of analysis (creatine, collagen, omega-3, kids' vitamins) and pitch it as cheaper than class-action defence. Sign one ISO 17025 lab for a fixed test panel. Run a public 'challenge week' with a supplement community, using a standard escrow account.

title: Phantom Load Vetting Desk for Rural Utilities
one_liner: A fee-based 'is this data center developer real?' diligence service for electric co-ops and municipal utilities drowning in 100-1,000 MW inquiries from shell LLCs.
customer: G&T and distribution electric cooperatives, municipal utilities and PUDs (5-person engineering staffs, no data center experience). Secondary: state economic development offices and county governments granting abatements. The utility or its G&T pays per inquiry or on retainer.
problem: Every small utility with transmission access is now getting inquiries for 200-1,000 MW campuses from LLCs formed 90 days ago. Each one eats study money, planning time and political capital, and a wrong bet strands ratepayer-funded infrastructure. Texas's proposed SB 6 rule (16 TAC 25.194, final rule due by end of 2026) would require $50,000/MW of financial security before a study and disclosure of duplicate requests. That pushes speculators into neighboring states and co-ops with softer tariffs. Small utilities have no way to tell a real project from a PowerPoint.
solution: A standardized 12-point 'physical reality' test built from paper trails that real projects leave and phantom ones cannot. (1) Air permit applications for generators, where the genset count implies the MW. (2) An OEM order acknowledgment or slot reservation for MV transformers and switchgear, plus a delivery date that fits the claimed energization date. (3) Recorded site control (deed or option). (4) Water and stormwater filings. (5) A named tenant LOI or offtaker. (6) A GC or EPC that has actually built a campus. (7) A financing letter. (8) Tax-abatement filings. (9) LLC principals cross-checked against other states' filings, to catch the same MW shopped to five utilities. (10) A power-density and cooling design consistent with the load ask. (11) Local land-use posture. (12) Team track record. The deliverable is a red/amber/green memo, a recommended security amount, and a milestone-gated study structure the utility can put in its ESA. Add-ons are a large-load tariff and ESA term-sheet template and a duplicate-request registry that co-ops in a region can pool.
why_now: Large-load tariffs and collateral rules are landing right now: Texas SB 6 (signed June 2025, PUCT rule proposed March 2026, final expected by 12/31/2026), plus AEP Ohio-style minimum-demand tariffs. Each new collateral regime displaces phantom load to the next-weakest utility. Transformer lead times of 3-5 years and switchgear sold out into 2028 mean that a real project without an equipment slot is not real, which gives a very cheap and reliable test. About half of announced 2026 builds are delayed or canceled, so utilities are burned and skeptical.
revenue_model: $7.5K-25K per inquiry vetting memo; $60K-150K/yr retainers for G&T co-ops that field 10+ inquiries a year; $25K-50K one-time tariff/ESA template packages; later a subscription to a multi-utility duplicate-request registry. Utilities can often pass the cost to the applicant as a study-deposit line item.
non_obvious_insight: Outsiders think the hard part of large-load planning is forecasting demand. Insiders know real projects are betrayed by equipment, not slides. A serious 300 MW developer has a transformer slot, a generator count on an air permit and a GC on payroll before the utility ever hears the name. A phantom has none of those. The tell is the logistics trail, and nobody at a 5-person co-op knows where to look. Texas's high collateral will also export the phantom problem to everyone else.
first_30_days: Build scrapers for state air-permit databases in 6-8 states and county deed/LLC records for 3 co-op service territories. Ask 3 co-op contacts (via state electric cooperative associations or a G&T's planning group) for their last 10 inquiries and run free back-tests on how they turned out. Publish a one-page '12 signs your data center inquiry is real' on LinkedIn and co-op association channels. Convert the first 2-3 into paid $7.5K memos on live inquiries and ask for a G&T retainer.

title: Live Doom-Pile Sessions for Avoided Paperwork
one_liner: A scheduled video session where a calm, admin-savvy host sits with you while you open the unopened mail pile, triages it, and gets the scary items handled before you hang up.
customer: Adults 25-55 with ADHD, anxiety, depression, recent bereavement or new-parent overload pay $59 per session or $89 a month for two sessions. Employer benefit programs, credit unions and probate attorneys pay for seats.
problem: Millions of people leave envelopes and portal notifications unopened because not knowing is more comfortable than knowing. Late fees, collections, missed renewals and tax notices escalate. The avoidance is emotional, so productivity apps and reminder tools do not touch it.
solution: A 45-minute weekly 'Admin Sunday' session. Members upload photos of the pile beforehand and AI produces a triage card (ignore, do this month, act by Friday). A trained host, such as a former paralegal, bookkeeper or benefits caseworker, sits with the member on camera as each envelope is opened. Three actions get done in the session, such as calling with a script, setting up a payment plan, or filing a form. The member leaves with a 'Nothing Scary' summary. A mail-forwarding tier serves people who cannot face even the session.
why_now: Adult ADHD diagnoses have surged and body-doubling is mainstream on TikTok and in tools like Focusmate. LLMs make triage and drafting nearly free, so one human can run 6-8 sessions a day and the business keeps a healthy margin. Collections on federal student loans restarted in 2025, raising the stakes of ignored mail. Consumers now value human presence precisely because AI can read the letter but cannot sit next to you.
revenue_model: $89 monthly subscription for two sessions, $59 a la carte. Hosts are paid $28-35 an hour, giving roughly 55-60% gross margin. B2B seats at $12-20 per employee per month for EAP and financial-wellness buyers.
non_obvious_insight: The product is courage with a witness, not productivity. People will pay to discover bad news in the company of someone calm. Silent co-working apps do not solve this because the body double is not allowed to help, and AI alone cannot absorb the emotion of opening the envelope.
first_30_days: Post in ADHD and adulting communities and make short 'doom pile' videos. Run 10 free consented live sessions to create content and testimonials. Sell $49 founding-member sessions through Stripe and run on Zoom and Google Drive. Recruit 5 hosts from retired paralegal and bookkeeper groups. Goal: 15 paying subscribers by day 30 and 30 by day 60.

title: Groundskeepers: Custodianship for AI-Built Software
one_liner: Property management for software: a monthly subscription where a named junior-developer 'groundskeeper' keeps small businesses' AI-built apps patched, backed up, monitored, and alive, with a senior signing off.
customer: SMBs (multi-location dentists, HVAC firms, property managers, boutique agencies) and solo founders who built internal tools or products with Lovable, Replit, Cursor and similar. $149-499/month per app. Agencies that built apps for clients can white-label.
problem: Building is free but owning is not. 'Vibe-code cleanup' is a recognized freelance niche, but it is a one-time project. After the rescue no one is responsible for dependency updates, key rotation, backups, uptime, model deprecations, and API changes, and a large share of production vibe-coded apps hit an incident within 90 days.
solution: A fixed-price move-in inspection ($900), then a monthly custody plan with monitoring, patching, backup verification, a lightweight quarterly security check, a runbook, and one accountable human with an incident SLA. Groundskeepers are laid-off junior developers, each managing 25-40 apps on a standardized template stack with AI tooling, supervised by fractional seniors. The plan includes an 'exit ramp' to rebuild or retire the app.
why_now: In 2026 a flood of AI-built apps entered production and cleanup specialists are one of the fastest-growing freelance niches, per Forbes coverage. Junior developer hiring has dried up, so skilled, cheap talent is abundant. Cyber insurers are beginning to care about managed versus unmanaged apps.
revenue_model: Recurring subscription, inspection fees, incident retainers, exit-ramp rebuilds, and referral fees from cyber insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The market frames this as cleanup (a project) but the durable business is custody (a relationship), like property management versus house flipping. The same structure gives displaced juniors a career ladder: custody is the residency that produces the senior engineers the industry stopped training.
first_30_days: Offer free move-in inspections to the first 20 apps through Lovable and Replit communities, local chambers of commerce, and SMB Facebook groups. Hire 2 laid-off juniors. Assemble monitoring from off-the-shelf tools (Sentry, uptime checks, Dependabot). Target 15 paying customers at about $199, roughly $3k monthly recurring revenue, by day 90.

title: Data Act Access-Request Desk for Independent Repairers
one_liner: A clearinghouse that files, tracks and escalates EU Data Act data-access requests to connected-product makers on behalf of independent garages, installers and fleet operators.
customer: Independent repair-shop networks, heat-pump and solar installers, agricultural-machinery service firms and small fleet operators (10-500 vehicles or machines) in the EU, plus their trade associations.
problem: Connected products must give users direct data access by design from 12 Sep 2026, and users can direct sharing to third parties. Every manufacturer will build its own portal, format and terms, and has every incentive to slow-walk independents. The EU repair directive transposition deadline (31 Jul 2026) also just passed. Small firms know wrenches, not statutory request letters or how to reach a national competent authority.
solution: A standardized request generator, a directory of each manufacturer's access method, a tracker with statutory-timeline reminders, normalization of the most-wanted data (fault codes, usage, battery health) and an escalation pack for the national authority. Launch with five manufacturers in two product categories.
why_now: The Data Act design obligation date was 12 Sep 2026, the repair directive deadline was 31 Jul 2026 and the EU repair platform is due 1 Jan 2028. Independents just received rights with no plumbing.
revenue_model: $49-149/month per shop, $5-20 per vehicle or machine per year for fleets, association licenses, and paid negotiation of bulk access terms.
non_obvious_insight: Compliance startups sell to the obligated party. The Data Act creates a beneficiary class that is fragmented and unsophisticated about law. The AirHelp pattern applies: rights that are costly to file individually but cheap to file collectively.
first_30_days: Sign two trade associations (independent aftermarket or agricultural repair). Send 20 manual requests across five OEMs and log response times, then publish an 'OEM Data Act responsiveness scorecard' to earn press and members. Charge $99/month.

title: Second Reader for Consumer Scan Anxiety
one_liner: An independent internist plus CBT-for-health-anxiety clinician who reads your Function, Superpower or full-body-scan results and tells you what not to chase.
customer: Members of consumer preventive-health services (blood-panel subscriptions and full-body scans), paying $99-199 per second read. Employers and the testing companies themselves come later, as white-label buyers, and only under a no-follow-up-revenue rule.
problem: Consumer preventive health is now mass market: Function has 1M+ members, Neko raised $700M for a NYC launch and Superpower just raised its price. Every result set produces borderline flags and incidental findings, which start cascades of retests and anxiety. The testing firms are diagnostic-only and paid on repeat testing, and their in-house clinicians are throughput-limited. Nobody is paid to say 'ignore this' or to treat the health anxiety the testing creates.
solution: A 45-minute second read by an internist, informed by radiology decision rules, ranks each finding as act, watch or ignore. A CBT-trained clinician adds a short protocol for uncertainty tolerance and reassurance-seeking. The member gets a one-page 'what not to chase' plan and a 30-day check-in, with optional monthly groups for chronic worriers. Simple decision trees for the top 30 flag types keep unit cost low.
why_now: Neko's US launch (July 2026), Function's $298M raise and acquisition of Ezra, and Superpower's Sep 2026 price increase are putting millions of first-time results in front of consumers at once. Mental health has been the top digital-health funding category for 7 years, so CBT clinicians are abundant and cheap to contract. LLM summaries make cheap first-pass triage possible, but they are not trusted with liability.
revenue_model: $99-199 per DTC second read, $19/month optional follow-up membership, and later a B2B2C white-label at about $6-12 per member per year to testing companies that want fewer refunds and complaints. Employers buy a capped-visit benefit.
non_obvious_insight: More testing creates a new patient, the worried well with abnormal-ish numbers, and testing companies are paid on the retest loop. An independent party paid by the patient has a credibility the vendor cannot fake. Health-anxiety CBT works, but anxious people seek doctors for reassurance, not therapists. Delivering it as a 'second opinion on your results' is the door they will walk through.
first_30_days: Contract two internists and one CBT-HA clinician part-time. Offer $99 founder-price second reads in Function and Superpower subreddits and longevity Discords. Run about 40 sessions and record pre/post anxiety scores (GAD-7 or Whiteley-7) and follow-up tests avoided. Take the outcome data to one scan center or one employer benefits broker.

title: Vet Tech Apprenticeship Intermediary
one_liner: Registered-apprenticeship sponsorship as a service, letting clinics grow their own technicians through a paid pathway with wage support and retention contracts.
customer: Clinics and groups with 3 or more open assistant or tech roles, plus state workforce boards that fund apprenticeships.
problem: Figures from a trade opinion piece (directional only): about 2 techs per vet versus a 4:1 ideal, most techs leave within 4 years, techs average about $45K, program enrollment is down 43%, and only about 7,000 of 14,000 needed new techs sit for licensing exams each year. Clinics cannot release staff for classroom time, and on-the-job training is unstructured.
solution: We register and manage an apprenticeship program as sponsor of record. Each apprentice pairs with an accredited distance-learning tech program, an on-site mentor (trained by us), a competency logbook and a wage-step schedule with a retention agreement. We file paperwork for state and workforce-board funds and track progress toward the licensing exam.
why_now: There is a 2025-26 push at the federal and state level to expand apprenticeships and fund workforce pathways (verify state programs). A new supervised professional tier (Colorado's VPA) raises demand for skilled support staff, and clinics are desperate for retention tools.
revenue_model: $250-400 per apprentice per month, a $500 clinic setup fee, and a share of state grants. Multi-clinic groups pay for program licenses.
non_obvious_insight: The shortage is discussed as 'not enough schools'. The real bottleneck is that employers cannot afford to release staff and have no retention hook. An apprenticeship converts an assistant already on payroll into a tech, with public money and a contract that keeps them.
first_30_days: Map which states permit apprenticeship or on-the-job routes to licensing and pick two. Get 3-5 clinics to commit 1-2 apprentices each. Partner with an accredited distance program. Begin state registration and charge a $500 setup fee to lock in clinics.

title: IEEPA Refund Ledger for CPAs and Controllers
one_liner: An accounting workbench that turns IEEPA refund data into correct inventory, cost-of-goods, tax and audit entries.
customer: CPA and advisory firms serving importers, and controllers at $10M-$500M manufacturers and distributors.
problem: About 330,000 importers paid about $166B on 53M entries. CBP had repaid about $86.3B by 2026-07-10, and AD/CVD and liquidated-entry cases come later. Each refund must be split between duty still in inventory, duty already in cost of goods sold, and interest, each with different book and tax treatment (UNICAP, state conformity, LIFO layers). CFOs have no playbook and brokers do not touch accounting.
solution: Import ACE entry-summary exports and broker data. Match each entry line to inventory layers or sales. Compute period-by-period reversal entries. Produce journal entries, a tax memo, a state schedule and a reconciliation to CBP statements. Model cash-tax timing for Q4 estimates. Export to QuickBooks, NetSuite and Sage.
why_now: Refunds are flowing in phases now, with year-end close and Q4 estimated payments (due 2026-12-15 for calendar-year C corporations) approaching.
revenue_model: $750-3k per client engagement through CPA firms. $15-40k a year for white-label licenses. It grows into a standing duty sub-ledger for Section 232 changes.
non_obvious_insight: A refund is an accounting event, not a customs event. Every refund creates an inventory-basis and tax problem the broker will not touch, and the same ledger becomes the duty sub-ledger firms need as Section 232 rates keep changing.
first_30_days: Approach 10 CPA firms with importer clients. Build an Excel and Python prototype on three real entry datasets. Sell the first engagements at about $1.5k. Have a tax partner review the methodology.

title: Paid Neighbor Walking Routes for Absent Kids
one_liner: Hire retired neighbors and parents as paid 'route captains' who walk or wake up chronically absent kids on fixed blocks, and get paid a share of the funding that the recovered attendance brings back.
customer: Principals and districts in states that fund schools on average daily attendance (California, Texas and similar). Secondary payers are city safe-passage budgets, Title I funds and Medicaid plans (for asthma and chronic-condition kids).
problem: About one in four kids is chronically absent. Nudge letters and text campaigns work on the 10 to 19 day group but barely touch the kids missing 25 or more days. For them it is a 7:40 a.m. logistics problem: a parent working an early shift, an older sibling who moved on to middle school, a dangerous corner, no clean clothes, no alarm clock. In attendance-funded states, each absent day costs the school roughly what a day of instruction is worth, so a $200-per-kid fix pays back several times over.
solution: Micro-employ 3 to 5 route captains per school as part-time W-2 workers (7:00 to 8:30 a.m., roughly $18 an hour). Each captain covers a block-by-block route, walking 6 to 10 kids, knocking on doors, and running a breakfast and laundry pass. Captains report barrier codes by voice note, which feed the attendance team's dashboard. Contract as a base route fee plus 20 to 25 percent of documented funding gains from improved attendance.
why_now: Chronic absenteeism has not returned to pre-pandemic levels. ESSER-funded attendance staff were cut as that money expired. States now require chronic-absence plans, and the retiree and gig-worker labor pool is looking for short, local, part-time work.
revenue_model: Base fee per route plus a performance share of recovered attendance funding. Optional per-route sponsorship from health plans or employers.
non_obvious_insight: Districts spend on software and letters, but the students who cost the most are the ones for whom the 7:40 a.m. logistics fail. The cheapest fix is a grandmother on the corner, and it is invisible to edtech buyers because it is not a product. The first three Mondays of September predict the year, so contracting has to start before October.
first_30_days: Pilot with one principal in an attendance-funded state: 2 routes, about 12 kids, 4 part-time captains recruited from churches and senior centers. Establish baselines from last year's attendance data and track days present weekly. Write the performance addendum as a one-page contract that a principal can sign with discretionary funds and later convert to a district contract.

title: Data Estate Broker for Main Street Closures
one_liner: An appraisal-and-brokerage service that finds, de-identifies and sells the operational exhaust (quotes, work orders, dispatch logs, inspection records) of retiring or closing non-tech firms to AI buyers.
customer: Owners, business brokers, insolvency practitioners and CPAs handling closures of small manufacturers, freight brokers, insurance agencies, energy contractors and engineering firms. The buyers are vertical-AI startups and labs that need real workflow data.
problem: Failed-company data is now valuable. Google bought bankrupt Spirit Airlines' data for $10M: 100M emails, 30M+ recorded calls, 763,000+ flights of ops data, 1.2M fuel slips and 787,452 parts purchases. Mercor was the underbidder. But SimpleClosure, the main shutdown broker, only serves VC-backed startups, whose H1 2026 shutdowns were 27.3% B2B SaaS and 14.4% AI. Buyers say they want scarce data from manufacturing, energy, banking, insurance, professional services and logistics. Those firms close or retire constantly and have nobody to appraise or sell their data.
solution: Start with operational, non-consumer-PII data, which is the least legally fraught. Examples are work orders, quotes and bids, dispatch and routing logs, inspection and maintenance records, CAD revision histories, and internal Q&A threads. Run a 'data asset scan' ($500-1,500, credited against fees), then rights review and de-identification. Package the results as licensed corpora, run a sealed-bid sale to vertical-AI buyers and take a 25-35% success fee. Recruit business brokers, liquidators and trade associations as referral partners. Consumer call recordings and customer emails are excluded until counsel signs off.
why_now: Buyers proved a price in Aug 2026 (Spirit, $10M) and there is a losing bidder waiting. SimpleClosure's own asset report shows buyers paying tens to hundreds of thousands for unique corpora and wanting 'how real work actually got done.' Vertical AI agents for trades and logistics need training data that does not exist on the open web. Small-business retirements are a multi-year wave, and Sherline Tools going out of business (Sept 2026) is one example.
revenue_model: 25-35% success fee on data licence sales, plus a $500-1,500 appraisal fee credited against it. Optional recurring 'living licence' fees for firms that stay open.
non_obvious_insight: The market for dead-company data exists, but the only broker is aimed at software startups, while buyers explicitly want boring industries. Evidence: Google's $10M Spirit purchase with Mercor as underbidder (https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/08/18/google-buys-crashed-airline-spirits-data-at-auction-because-ai/5288962). The HN discussion notes that Scale, Surge and Mercor are recreating workplace data (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49343559). SimpleClosure's asset report lists 'manufacturing, energy, banking, insurance, professional services, logistics' as scarce-data buyers (https://simpleclosure.com/blog/insights/what-your-assets-are-worth/). Its H1 2026 report shows its funnel is startups (https://simpleclosure.com/blog/insights/state-of-shutdowns-h1-2026/). The main risk is privacy backlash. HN commenters doubt the de-identification ('I'm skeptical it'll be wiped correctly'), so the wedge is operational data with no consumer PII.
first_30_days: Week 1: pick two verticals, for example machine shops and freight brokerage. Book 20 calls with business brokers and CPAs who handle closures. Weeks 2-3: sign 3 exclusive listing agreements on a free data-asset scan. Line up 5 buyer LOIs from vertical-AI startups building quoting or dispatch agents. Week 4: complete one appraisal, get a privacy-counsel template for rights review, and run the first sealed-bid process.

title: Tooling Hostage: Repatriate Molds and Dies
one_liner: Extract molds, dies and fixtures from Asian suppliers, refurbish them, and re-home them with US or nearshore shops.
customer: Consumer-product and industrial OEMs with $10M-$500M revenue and $50k-$2M of tooling sitting at Asian contract manufacturers, plus the new US or Mexican shops that will use it.
problem: Tariffs, a USMCA that was not renewed, and a war shock (freight up to 50%) push companies to move production. The first blocker is the tooling. Ownership is ambiguous, suppliers demand payoffs, drawings are missing, and nobody handles inspection, crating, freight and requalification as one service.
solution: Step 1 is a fixed-fee Tool Audit covering contract review, inspection video, location, condition and cost to escape. Step 2 is turnkey extraction: a local agent and letter, crating, freight and a customs review of the tooling's duty class. Step 3 is US refurbishment and first-article requalification through partner shops. Step 4 is a scan-and-drawing escrow so the next move is easy.
why_now: Companies are re-sourcing now under the rebuilt tariff regime. Freight and war-risk surcharges make each move costly, and the first-mover on tool logistics is unclaimed territory.
revenue_model: Audit at $2.5-5k. Extraction at $8-40k or 10-15% of tooling value. Refurbishment and requalification pass-through at about 15% margin. Escrow subscription.
non_obvious_insight: The lock-in in Asia is the tool, not cheap labor, and the tool's legal owner is often unclear. Whoever holds the tool controls the reshoring decision, so extraction is the real first step. Duty treatment of imported tooling and Chinese export or IP disputes need counsel.
first_30_days: Publish a 'Where are your tools?' checklist. Run 5 audits for hardware brands found via trade shows and Amazon brand lists. Hire a fixer and lawyer in Shenzhen or Ningbo. Line up one refurbishment partner shop in Ohio or Michigan.

title: Celebration-of-Life Concierge Using Restaurants' Dead Hours
one_liner: A flat-fee, turnkey memorial-gathering service for families who buy a cheap direct cremation and then have to improvise a goodbye, hosted in restaurants, breweries and hotel rooms during their empty weekday hours.
customer: Adult children (45-65) who bought direct cremation and must host 40-100 guests. Distribution partners are low-cost direct-cremation providers and hospice bereavement teams. Venues (restaurants, breweries, event rooms) pay a commission for filled dead hours.
problem: Funeral homes are hated for opaque upselling, so families flee to direct cremation at roughly $1,000-$3,000. That unbundles the ceremony: the gathering still happens 2-6 weeks later, but nobody provides it. Families scramble to find a venue, catering, a slideshow, an officiant and a livestream for remote relatives, while the cremation provider has no product for the moment that most shapes the family's memory of them.
solution: One booking that covers venue, per-head menu, host or officiant, memory-board and slideshow, RSVP and guest messaging, livestream and a printed program. The family pays a flat planning fee. The venue keeps the food and beverage revenue and pays a commission. Cremation providers and hospices embed a link in their after-care emails and take a referral fee or white-label it as their own add-on. A vetted list of local celebrants and photographers sits underneath.
why_now: The US cremation rate reached about 63.4% in 2025 and direct cremation is the fastest-growing disposition. NFDA reports that a majority of people have attended a funeral event at a non-traditional location, so the behavior has already shifted while the supply side is still a patchwork of ad hoc rentals. Restaurants and breweries are hunting for private-event revenue in weekday afternoons.
revenue_model: Family pays $750-$1,500 planning fee, plus add-ons (livestream, officiant, printed programs). Venue pays 12-15% of the food and beverage minimum (a 60-guest gathering at $55-$80 a head is $3-5k of spend). Referral fee of about $100 per booking to cremation providers and hospices.
non_obvious_insight: The funeral industry unbundled its own most emotional and highest-margin product. Disposition is now a commodity, but the ceremony did not disappear; it moved two to six weeks later, out of the funeral home, into a category no one owns, and it comes with a no-panic timeline, so the family is willing to plan and spend on it. The scarce resource is not a chapel, it is a trusted person who takes care of the whole afternoon.
first_30_days: Pick one high-cremation metro (Portland, Seattle, Las Vegas or Phoenix). Sign 8-10 venues with private rooms and per-head menus. Get two direct-cremation providers and two hospice bereavement coordinators to send a 'what happens next' link to families. Run the first gatherings by hand with a shared calendar, a phone line and a single landing page. The first paid bookings should come through partner referrals within weeks, and the service can stay fully concierge until 30-40 gatherings show what to automate.

title: Water Due Diligence for Small-Business Acquisitions
one_liner: A 5-day, fixed-price water-risk report for buyers, lenders and brokers of car washes, farms, RV parks, breweries and other water-dependent small businesses, plus a sell-side 'water-ready' file.
customer: Independent searchers and SBA buyers, business brokers and SBA lenders on $500k-$10M deals in water-dependent SMBs: car washes, farms, orchards and vineyards, RV parks and campgrounds, breweries and distilleries, nurseries, laundromats, ice and bottled-water plants, mobile-home parks.
problem: The Boomer sale wave meets drought. The value of these businesses rests on a tap, a well or a priority date that nobody puts in the sale memo. Phase I environmental assessments do not cover water rights, capacity, curtailment or PFAS and nitrate exposure. Buyers are first-timers with no diligence infrastructure. Search-fund capital targets $5-50M, and sub-$1M cash-flow businesses have no comparable formal capital.
solution: A 10-page report covering the legal water source and priority date, well permit and yield history, utility will-serve letter, capacity and moratoria, tap and system development fees, discharge and pretreatment permits, source-water quality against 2027 PFAS monitoring and nitrate, drought-surcharge exposure, a curtailment scenario under the Colorado River framework or state freezes, and an EBITDA-at-risk and price-adjustment table. A contract hydrogeologist reviews and LLMs assist with records pulls. Sell-side version: a $900 'water-ready' file that defends price.
why_now: From 2026-07-04 an SBA 7(a) loan can be combined with a 504 loan for up to $10M, so more real-estate-heavy deals will close. The Colorado River decision (Aug 2026) and Texas's Aug 3 grid freeze show that water and utility access can now stop a business. PFAS initial monitoring lands in 2027. 49.6% of the US is in drought. First-time buyers have no template for any of it.
revenue_model: $1,800-$3,500 per buy-side report. $900 per sell-side file. $299/mo broker pre-screen subscription. Bulk per-deal rate for SBA lenders. Referral fees from acquisition attorneys.
non_obvious_insight: Drought risk in a water-tied business is binary, not gradual. One curtailment or moratorium takes terminal value near zero, yet brokers, lenders and CPAs price it at zero. Whoever can put a number on the tap gets paid by buyers (walk away or reprice) and by sellers (defend the price). Once one bank asks for it, it becomes a checkbox for every SBA deal in the region.
first_30_days: Pick two states. Contract a hydrogeologist or water attorney for the review step. Go to 10 business brokers who specialize in car washes, farms and RV parks and offer 5 free reports on live listings. Ask two SBA lender loan officers to trial it. Convert 3 to paid at $2,500 by day 60.

title: Translator-Owned Language Trusts for Public Services
one_liner: Translator co-ops that build and license verified medical, legal, and benefits corpora for refugee and diaspora languages, and sell certified human review to agencies that now rely on machine translation.
customer: State Medicaid and benefits agencies, hospital systems, courts, and school districts serving speakers of Karen, Somali, Kirundi, Tigrinya, Haitian Creole, Hmong, Dari, and similar languages. Agencies pay per-word review and $50-150k annual contracts. AI labs and voice-AI vendors license evaluation and fine-tuning data.
problem: General translation is commoditized, so translators are displaced. But in low-resource languages, machine translation of consent forms, discharge instructions, and benefits notices is wrong in dangerous ways, and agencies use it because human capacity has evaporated. Translators' glossaries and corrections are given away or locked in agency-owned translation memories, and gig data platforms pay a pittance.
solution: A member-owned trust per language cluster. Translators contribute and verify domain glossaries and parallel corpora under community governance with consent, revenue share, and veto rights. The trust sells (a) certified human review of machine-translated public-service documents with a warranty, (b) benchmarks and licensed data to vendors, with usage royalties passed to members, and (c) an MT-plus-human-guardrails workflow for agencies.
why_now: The HHS Section 1557 rule (2024) requires qualified human review when machine translation is used on critical health documents, and it remains in effect in 2026, which creates non-discretionary demand. The Mozilla Data Collective opened paid commercial licensing of community datasets and the Gates Foundation has committed to language AI. Freelance translation rates have collapsed.
revenue_model: Per-word certified-review fees, annual agency retainers, data and benchmark licenses, and patronage dividends to member translators.
non_obvious_insight: A translator's most valuable asset is not their time but their error corrections in narrow domains, which is precisely what every model is worst at. The co-op structure solves both community trust and individual freelancers' lack of bargaining power, and legal language-access duties turn the buyer's budget from discretionary to mandatory.
first_30_days: Pick one language and one metro with a large diaspora, such as Karen speakers in St. Paul. Recruit 10-15 translators as founding members. Offer a hospital system or county health department a paid pilot to review its top 50 patient documents against Section 1557 requirements. Build the glossary in shared tooling and sign a governance charter.

title: The 40 Days: Postpartum Confinement Caregiver Guild
one_liner: A trained, insured, tradition-certified caregiver guild delivering the 26 to 42 day postpartum confinement (yuesao, sanhujori, cuarentena) to diaspora families whose grandmothers are far away.
customer: New parents in Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese, South Asian, Latino and Middle Eastern communities in dense metros, mostly mothers at 30 to 36 weeks. Secondary payers: extended-family gift funds and employers or health plans looking to reduce postpartum depression.
problem: Confinement care is widely practiced but supplied through informal agencies and word of mouth. A US yuesao runs about $200 to $400 a day for the standard 26 days, and a 42-day term adds roughly 60%. Quality, safety and worker protections vary widely, agencies rarely serve non-Chinese traditions, and parents without a grandmother nearby are left choosing between exhaustion and a gray-market caregiver.
solution: Build the guild rather than a marketplace. Recruit experienced caregivers and give them W-2 employment, insurance and background checks, plus training in safe sleep, lactation basics, infection control and postpartum warning signs with an escalation path to the family's OB or midwife. Certify them in specific traditions (menus, do's and don'ts) and match on language and tradition. Sell modular tiers: nights only, meals only, 14, 28 or 42 days. Add a plain-language guide for in-laws and partners.
why_now: Immigrant-heavy metros have a large unmet pool of families who want the ritual, and grandmothers are harder to bring over given tighter visa and travel rules. Employer-of-record and payroll tools make W-2 caregiver employment easy for a tiny company. Postpartum mental health is a rising priority for employers and health plans.
revenue_model: $5,500 to $12,000 per family per engagement, at about 30% to 35% gross margin after caregiver pay. Meals-only tier at $35 to $55 a day for faster revenue. Employer or plan subsidy of $1,000 to $2,000 per birth. A gift registry for extended family.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input is the trusted caregiver, so the moat is a certified workforce (training, payroll, insurance, safety escalation), not a listing site. Confinement is also the same intervention American medicine now calls the fourth trimester, so obstetric practices can refer to it without endorsing folk claims, and it has been an informal cash market that has never been professionalized.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with a dense Chinese-American or Korean-American community such as the San Gabriel Valley, Flushing or the Bay Area. Recruit 8 experienced caregivers through WeChat groups and existing agencies. Write a three-day training and safety protocol with a postpartum nurse and lactation consultant. Sign 10 founding families with a service guarantee, and sell a meals-only tier to 50 families for faster revenue. Line up two OB practices or doulas for referrals, and set up employer-of-record payroll.

title: Tariff Refund Liquidation-Cliff Radar
one_liner: A deadline tracker and filing generator for small importers and small customs brokers that tells them, entry by entry, which refund route is still open and when it closes.
customer: Importers with 200-20,000 entries per year, and independent customs brokers serving them, who lack in-house trade counsel. Priced per entry or as a success fee.
problem: CBP will not refund automatically. Filers must act through CAPE, a Post Summary Correction (PSC) or a protest, and each route has a different window. CAPE Phase 1 accepts only unliquidated entries or entries liquidated in the preceding 80 days. Protests must be filed within 180 days of liquidation. PSCs must be filed within 300 days of entry or 15 days before liquidation. Finally liquidated entries, drawback, TIB and reconciliation entries are ineligible. The importer also needs ACE Portal access and ACH enrollment on file. Any outstanding CBP debt is offset first under 19 CFR 24.72.
solution: The tool ingests the ACE entry summary and liquidation reports (ES-003 or ES-022 exports, or a broker CSV). It assigns every IEEPA-duty entry a status and route (CAPE-eligible now, protest-only, PSC window, ineligible) and a hard 'last day' date. It auto-builds CAPE declaration files (up to 9,999 entries) for the broker and protest packets for the rest. It reconciles ACH deposits and interest against the ACE refund reports (REV-603 and REV-615) so the finance team can book the refund entry by entry. It flags CBP-debt offsets and scam solicitations, since CBP has warned about fraudsters targeting refund claimants.
why_now: The rolling cliff is live. Every month another vintage of 2025 entries liquidates, and each has a fresh 80-day CAPE window and a 180-day protest window that can lapse silently. Refunds are being recognised in one lump. AutoZone's alone was worth $4.43 EPS in a quarter. Auditors will require entry-level tie-outs.
revenue_model: $3-8 per entry tracked, $25K-$75K annual site licences for small brokers with 50+ importer clients, or a 3-5% success fee on refunds recovered from entries that would otherwise have gone finally liquidated.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is a calendar, not law-firm expertise. CBP's own pages say 'ACE accepts CAPE Declarations containing entries liquidated within the preceding 80 days', 'once an entry has liquidated, a protest may be filed within 180 days', and 'you cannot remove entries from the Declaration' once filed (https://www.cbp.gov/trade/programs-administration/trade-remedies/ieepa-duty-refunds and https://www.cbp.gov/trade/programs-administration/trade-remedies/IEEPA-FAQ). CBP says only the IOR or its broker can file, and the FAQ never mentions automatic refunds. Public companies are already booking eight-figure refunds (AutoZone about $96M, MillerKnoll $16.5M, Worthington $4M: https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/23/worthington-wor-q1-2027-earnings-call-transcript/). The long tail of small importers is running on broker email chains and is the most likely to lose entries to a missed window.
first_30_days: Cold-email and call 100 independent customs brokers (from NCBFAA and local port broker lists) with an offer: 'send us your entry list and we'll return a route-and-deadline sheet within 24 hours, free'. Build the classifier in a spreadsheet plus a Python script. Publish a public liquidation-date calculator as a lead magnet aimed at importers. Convert the first 3 brokers to a paid per-entry contract, and have each refer 5-10 importer clients.

title: Deferred-Payment Shield for Grain Sellers
one_liner: A counterparty-risk monitor plus surety/letter-of-credit wrap that turns the unsecured December 'deferred payment' loans farmers unknowingly make to their elevators into protected receivables.
customer: Row-crop operators with 2,000+ acres who each defer $400k to $2M of grain revenue into January, and the ag lenders and farm CPAs who advise them. Co-ops and elevators with strong balance sheets are a secondary payer, because the wrap becomes a way to win bushels.
problem: Every November and December, farmers sign deferred payment contracts to push income into next year for tax reasons. Most think they are just delaying a check. Legally, title has passed and they are unsecured creditors of the buyer. Iowa's Grain Indemnity Fund gives deferred payment contracts zero coverage. Deferred pricing ('price later') contracts get 75% coverage capped at $400,000 per claimant. Farm balance sheets are stretched, so more farmers are lending large sums to buyers they have never vetted.
solution: Start with a free 'Elevator Exposure Report'. The farmer lists every open contract, prepaid input balance and stored-grain receipt. The tool compares total exposure with the Fund's actual coverage and scores each buyer using licensing status, audit history, buyer size, and settlement-timing behavior reported by users. Then sell the fix. A specialty MGA or bank issues a surety bond or standby letter of credit against the buyer's payment promise, structured with ag tax counsel so tax deferral is preserved. The fee is roughly 0.3% to 0.8% of face value. Ag lenders subscribe to a portfolio dashboard showing how much of their borrowers' grain receivables sit with weak buyers.
why_now: Chapter 12 farm bankruptcies rose 46% in 2025 and April 2026 hit a six-year high. USDA projects record farm debt of about $625B in 2026. The 2025 bumper crop and low prices pushed farmers toward deferral and storage. The 2026 December deferral season opens in about 90 days, which is a hard deadline for a first pilot.
revenue_model: Wrap fee split with the surety or LC provider (0.3% to 0.8% of contract face value). Ag lender portfolio-monitoring subscription ($1k to $5k a month per lender). Optional $299 per farm annual exposure audit sold through CPAs.
non_obvious_insight: The elevator that pushes deferred payment contracts hardest in November is often the one that needs your cash, because deferrals are free working capital for a thinly capitalized buyer. Farmers think of the elevator as a warehouse. Once title passes, it is a borrower. Nobody rates that borrower.
first_30_days: Build the exposure calculator as a free web form and scorecard from Iowa Dept. of Ag license data and public filings. Get 5 farm CPAs and 3 rural banks to run their biggest clients through it. Sign one surety broker or bank willing to quote wraps, and target 10 paid wraps before the December deferral rush.

title: Persistent Methane Plumes as Equipment Sales Leads
one_liner: Sell satellite-detected methane emitters to the vendors who profit from fixing them: a lead-gen engine, not a compliance tool.
customer: Vapor-recovery-unit makers, flare-gas-to-power microturbine and genset vendors, landfill gas-collection contractors, dairy digester and RNG developers, and small gas gatherers or offtakers. Roughly 2,000 companies in the US; first buyers are sales VPs at 20-person equipment firms.
problem: Abatement vendors prospect blind at trade shows. Emitters are often unaware of a persistent leak or vent, or they do not know its dollar value. A 500 kg/h plume is roughly 230,000 MMBtu a year, or about $0.7M of saleable gas at $3/MMBtu. Methane data today is sold to regulators, ESG buyers and the emitters themselves, and none of them are motivated.
solution: A weekly ranked lead list of persistent emitters, defined as repeated detections across passes from open Carbon Mapper, EMIT and Tanager plume products, with GHGSat tasking to confirm the best leads. Each lead joins the plume to facility ownership (state permits, landfill and EPA datasets), wasted-gas value per year, distance to pipeline or grid, and likely fix type. Delivered as a CRM feed plus a one-page dossier.
why_now: Plume data is now abundant and partly free: Carbon Mapper's Tanager publishes public plume products, and GHGSat is expanding to 16+ satellites. With US federal methane-penalty pressure pushed out, pitches built on fines are weak, while pitches built on recovering saleable gas still work. Cheap gas-to-power gensets and microturbines are also more available.
revenue_model: $2k to $6k a month per vendor per basin or vertical. Success fee of 2% to 4% of first-year equipment or service revenue on closed leads, capped. Later, sell offtake and RNG-interconnect leads to gas buyers.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone treats a methane plume as a violation to be reported. It is really an unmonetized commodity with a known street address and a quantifiable price. Selling the plume to the person who profits from fixing it inverts the market and does not depend on regulation.
first_30_days: Pull open plume data for the Permian, Appalachia and Ohio/Pennsylvania landfills and build the top 100 persistent emitters. Hand-verify ownership and gas value on each. Cold-offer 25 equipment vendors and landfill gas contractors three free leads, then $3k a month. Ask for a paid pilot from 3 by day 30.

title: Referee Body-Cams and Abuse Evidence Layer
one_liner: A clip-on camera and incident-report service that gives youth and high school officials proof and gives leagues grounds to ban abusive spectators.
customer: State high school associations, officials' associations, youth leagues and tournament operators, paying per official per season.
problem: About 50,000 high school officials have left since 2018, more than 70 percent of new referees quit within three years, and half report feeling unsafe. Insiders assume pay raises fix the shortage, but abuse is the driver and leagues cannot sanction parents or coaches without evidence, so games run short-staffed or get cancelled.
solution: A $50-100 chest-mounted camera or phone clip with audio; speech-to-text flags threats and slurs; league admins get a one-click incident packet (timestamps, transcript, clip) tied to a spectator code of conduct; officials get a private 'safe report' button. Leagues use the evidence to issue bans and support refs.
why_now: 2026 shortage coverage (New York, Utah and others) consistently blames abuse; cheap on-device transcription and body cams make this a $60 problem; national bodies such as USA Volleyball have created formal harassment-response programs, showing appetite.
revenue_model: $40-90 per official per season (hardware included) plus $500-3k per year per league for the admin dashboard; potential insurer partnerships.
non_obvious_insight: The shortage is a safety problem, not a pay problem, and the true buyer is the league's risk manager. Recording laws vary by state, so the product is policy-first (posted notices, opt-in associations) and starts where the association mandates it.
first_30_days: Pilot with one regional officials association (about 100 officials) using off-the-shelf action cams and a transcription pipeline, draft a spectator-policy template with a local attorney, run one season of evidence, and convert two leagues into paying customers.
